title: Correlative confocal and scanning electron microscopy of cultured cells without using dedicated equipment
protocol: Cover the surface of the inset of a glass-bottomed 35 mm Petri dish with 650 μL of 0.1% (wt/vol) poly-L-lysine solution and incubate for 30 min at 37°C.
Rinse with deionized water.
Air-dry in a fume hood to keep the coverslip surface clean.
Vortex the Au NPs stock thoroughly before use.
Sonicate the Au NPs suspension in a bath sonicator for 3 cycles of 30 seconds each.
Dilute the Au NPs suspension to achieve a final density of 1–5 × 10^4 particles mm^-2 on the coverslip surface.
Add 650 μL of diluted Au NPs suspension to the inset.
Incubate at 37°C for 2 hours.
Retire the remaining solution after incubation.
Air-dry the sample.
Mark the bottom of the coverslip with an ethanol-resistant marker to orient the sample.
Sterilize the dish previously coated with Au NPs by exposing it to a germicide lamp for 15–30 min.
Add 2 mL of MDCK cells expressing desired fluorescent fusion proteins (7.5 × 10^4/mL) suspended in MEM to the plate.
Culture the cells for 48–72 h at 37°C in an atmosphere of 5% CO2.
Ensure that the culture is subconfluent at the time of fixing.
Adjust the initial number of cells and duration of culturing phase accordingly.
Mix a volume of 2× fixing solution equal to the volume of culture medium in the dish.
Incubate for 10 minutes at room temperature (RT; 20°C–22°C).
Remove most of the liquid and add fresh 1× fixing solution.
Incubate for 2 h at 20°C–22°C or 8–10 h at 4°C.
Substitute fixing solution with phosphate buffer 0.1 M.
Place the dish on the sample stage, using marks as a reference.
Acquire a large field-of-view image for alignment and navigation purposes.
Include fluorescence signals and reflection channel showing Au NPs in the image acquisition.
Perform imaging at the center of the coverslip if possible.
Generate images by acquiring a 10 × 10 tilescan z-stack with specified parameters.
Optimize acquisition settings based on the abundance and signal strength of the structure of interest.
Perform all confocal imaging in one session to maintain sample orientation consistency.
Acquire medium-FOV (100 × 100 μm) images including fluorescence signals and reflection channel showing Au NPs.
Include an area with exposed substrate near the structures of interest when selecting the imaging region.
Keep track of medium-FOV image positions relative to the large-FOV image.
Re-center the stage to a given position on a previously acquired image when using a motorized stage.
Annotate the position of each medium-FOV image on an additional copy of the large-FOV image.
Record the objective position relative to the coverslip during imaging.
Take a picture of the stage adaptor during the imaging session for reference.
Make an ethanol-resistant mark on the backside of the coverslip at the imaged area.
Pause point: Store samples for up to one week at 4°C in 1× fixing solution after phosphate buffer substitution.
Alternatively, store samples in PBS with antibacterial agents added.
Open the large-FOV image in ImageJ.
Perform a z-projection and create a compressed jpeg version of the large-FOV confocal image.
Highlight and identify the regions that correspond to each medium-FOV image on the large-FOV image.
Identify candidate structures present inside the highlighted regions.
Remove most of the liquid from the dish.
Turn the dish upside-down and add some drops of acetone around the perimeter of the coverslip.
Incubate for 5–10 s.
Clean any remaining acetone.
Following buffer removal, turn the dish upside-down and add acetone around the perimeter of the coverslip.
Apply uniform pressure from the sample-side on the coverslip using a hollow cylinder with a slightly smaller diameter than the inset.
Alternatively, introduce a scalpel between the coverslip and plastic and gently rotate the dish to liberate the coverslip.
Place the detached coverslip (sample facing up) quickly on a 6-well plate with phosphate buffer.
Immerse the samples in increasing concentrations of ethanol starting with 10%, increasing by 10% increments up to 100%, incubating for 3 minutes per solution.
Incubate samples in a 1:1 mixture of ethanol and HMDS for 3 minutes after reaching 100% ethanol.
Incubate samples in pure hexamethyldisilazane (HMDS) for 3 minutes.
Remove all liquid from the dish and air-dry on the fume hood overnight.
Mount the sample on the SEM stub using thin conductive double-sided tape (carbon) with cells attached to the upper side.
Align reference marks made during coating and gold fiducial marker addition section with the stub to maintain orientation.
Place the sample on the holder using the reference marks.
Introduce the sample into the SEM chamber.
Frame the edges of the glass substrate with metallic tape, avoiding the area imaged by confocal microscopy.
Place the stub on the SEM stage holder and introduce it into the SEM chamber.
Align the sample with the microscope motion axis using the reference marks.
Navigate to the surface features identified by confocal microscopy.
Set the working conditions for the electron beam to a desired working distance of 4 mm.
Use very low voltage and low current, recommended between 0.5–1 kV and 13–25 pA respectively, to minimize charge effects.
Align the column carefully.
Acquire a large-FOV image that is approximately 2 mm wide and around 50x magnification for comparison with the look-up map.
Use either in-chamber or in-lens SE detectors for acquiring the large-FOV image.
Choose beam dwell times around 1–3 μs as charge effects are minimal at this low magnification.
Compare confocal and SEM large-FOV images for relevant structures.
Identify occasional defects in the images.
Correct the sample's position and orientation if necessary.
Start identifying sections of interest using the look-up map.
Acquire medium-FOV images with dimensions of 100 μm wide at around 1,000× magnification.
Adjust dwell times to be within the range of 100–300 ns for optimal image quality.
Ensure imaged area matches that of the medium-FOV confocal microscopy images obtained previously.
Use in-lens secondary electrons detector for better resolution in medium-FOV imaging.
Increase image resolution if necessary based on size of structures of interest.
Employ a pixel definition of 3072∗2048 for high-resolution observation of Au NPs and surface features.
Identify regions of interest using confocal and SEM medium-FOV images.
Localize Au NPs based on their pattern formation.
Acquire small-FOV SEM images at magnifications between 10,000×−100,000× with the in-lens SE detector.
Use FOV width of around 2–5 μm and magnifications between 25,000×−60,000× for imaging midbody remnants.
Set low-dwell times (50–100 ns) to reduce charge effects during high-magnification imaging.
Frame integrate images with software drift correction activated to improve signal-to-noise ratio.
Tilt and rotate the sample stage as needed to obtain views from different orientations.
Acquire images in the same conditions used for initial imaging.
Open medium-FOV confocal and SEM images on ImageJ.
Adjust brightness and contrast if needed.
Find the structure of interest in both images.
Crop a region around the structure, including closest Au NPs, in both images.
Generate final confocal image by selecting desired planes and making projections.
Split channels and save each as a different TIFF file.
Start a new TrakEM2 project.
Link all the images in the "Confocal" layer.
Make visible only the channel containing the Au NPs.
Use the “link” (chain) and “visibility” (eye) icons to link and make visible the relevant channels.
Register both images using the Au NPs as manual landmarks by right-clicking on the canvas, selecting align, then align layers manually with landmarks.
Select the Au NPs near the feature of interest one by one in the same order.
Align both images by “similarity” by right-clicking on the canvas, selecting apply transform, model: similarity, and propagating to the first layer.
Scale the images to match pixel size with the high magnification SEM image.
